utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This morning we only have two sittings, like yesterday. And we'll finish the direct examination of this witness by the Prosecution, whichever is earlier. Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me? Your microphone. Yes, would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to start by asking the usher to hand you a piece of paper that has your name on it, I believe. We can do that momentarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I should just indicate, Your Honours, that I will be asking to go into private session on a couple of occasions during the process of the examination-in-chief with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you, please, look at that piece of paper and tell us whether or not that's your name without saying it out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: This is my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That, for the record, is marked as P-3406.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Perhaps we can just start with some background information, sir. Are you from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether you're -- are you Muslim by faith, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And could you please explain to the Judges your educational background.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Your Honours, I finished high school in 1981. Then I completed my training as an electrician in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that you have an interest in radios. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. I was intensively involved in hand radio operation ever since I was 17. Also, I constructed radio amateur devices -- radio devices as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And do you have any types of special classifications or certificates that you received in your pursuit of your interest in radios?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. In 1977 I received what is called a C classification for radio amateurs. In 1984 I obtained a B category, as it is called. This is a professional category.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, starting with the C classification, could you explain to us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The C category involves receiving telegraph signals, 60 signals per minute, then also being familiar with the so-called prefixes that are country codes, actually. Then also abbreviations that are used for the formation of a telegraph conversation. And also a solid knowledge of electronics.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned that in 1984 you received your B category exam. Can you explain to us what that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just want to bring to the Court's attention that the Prosecutor is leading for the witness, but for basic information we will allow her to lead the witness until it gets to the substance of the conflicts that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, this is background information. In this situation, leading questions are allowed, otherwise we will spend the whole day here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation, Ms. Sinatra. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what that is, sir, what a B classification is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The B category means receiving telegraph signs, 80 signs per minute, considerably more extensive knowledge of electronics than for the C category. Then also a considerably larger number of abbreviations and codes for telegraph conversations and a considerably larger number of country codes that are called prefixes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And I understand, sir, that in 1982 before you received your B classification, you joined the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in active service of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I was in active service for 14 months, and that is where I obtained a military C category for telegraphs and teleprinters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And did you have a particular specialty while you were in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. During my training, I used the MKSK, this was a small command communication vehicle. And later on when I went to the command of the boarder outposts, then I used telegraph teleprinter devices, operated them, radio teleprinter devices, the one that is called radio teleprinter 100. RTU-100. That is what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And in the course of your service with the JNA, were there any other devices or types of radio devices that you became familiar with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. There were others, many other devices. For example, the RUP-12, the RUP-15 then the RDM-66 I'm sorry 63. Then radio telephones 66/17, 66/3, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Can you very briefly in general terms just explain to us what those devices mean, the names that you have just told us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The names themselves refer to the frequency of the device concerned or the year when it was manufactured. For example, the RUP-15 is a short wave radio device. It's a transmitter and receiver. The RUP-12 is ultra short wave transmitter of 30 to 60 megahertz [as interpreted]. I forgot to mention that the RUP-15 is from 2 to 15 megahertz. Then the radio telephone, the 66/17 type. It has 17 channels. It was manufactured in 1966, 10 watts, and it works at a frequency of 150 megahertz, and so on and so forth. I forgot to mention that at the exchange within our unit where I was in this other period during my service in the army, at the telephone exchange, we had devices that are called frequency bearers, 12K type.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did you maintain your interest in radios until the time the conflict started in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. I intensively worked as a radio amateur, because at first I did not have a job after my army service. And I could devote more time to that part of my hobby. I bought myself a short wave transmitter of my own and then a small pocket-sized ultra short wave one, so that was about it. But these were my private radio stations. I had my private radio amateur code.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Issa, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's all right, Your Honour. I was actually going to ask that we go to private session at this point as it may transgress the areas of the protections at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned that the purpose or one of the purposes of your unit was to monitor enemy communications. Can you tell us who you're referring to, who you were monitoring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I have understood the period that your question pertains or to perhaps it is a general question, so that's why I'm going to give the following answer: It was necessary to prevent electronic attacks -- I beg your pardon. It was necessary to prevent electronic operations during an enemy attack. And it was necessary to gain all possible knowledge about enemy movements and material and technical equipment. It was necessary to obtain this kind of information so that the command could, on the basis of other sources as well, intelligence information, check out what the situation was actually like, to see what the situation was within enemy ranks and to have as much information as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we'll just get back to that. Did you remain, sir, in the field of - perhaps I should put it this way - anti-electronic warfare until the conclusion of the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you've just described to us what the -- let me ask you this. What is the purpose specifically of intercepting enemy communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Basically the objective is to know as much as possible about the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And to your knowledge, sir, did the other parties to the war, the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Serbs, the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia also have some type of anti-electronic warfare unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to including the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So far there's been no evidence in this case that they were engaged in this war. Milosevic is being tried in another courtroom, not in this one. So I object to that. I don't object to the other with respect to the Bosnian Serbs or the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, this is a very general question, very general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, I understand. I'm a stickler for the details, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I support Mr. Karnavas's objection, but the fact is that Ms. Issa has not asked who was the enemy. She just made a list in her question proposed to the witness. Now, I think it needs to come to him who he recognised as the enemy in 1992 and 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did we mention the matter of the enemy? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I think -- she asked him earlier who the enemy was and he didn't answer the question and now she's listed people who he considers that they're fighting against. I believe the witness has not answered the question originally posed by Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Issa just said the other parties to the war, which is very general.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I was just asking to have the opinion of the witness as to who the other parties of the war. It's not strictly the two parties involved in this case right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, there's some reason in your objection. Well, Ms. Issa, first establish who are the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I didn't think that was in dispute particularly, but I can certainly ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, who are the other parties to the war at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The other parties have just been mentioned in the previous question, right, and I'm going to give you a concrete answer in order to make things simpler for you, whether the other parties had a unit for electronic warfare. I'm going to be quite clear on this point. The Bosnian Serbs did have this unit. That is exactly the answer I want to give.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But the question to you, sir, and I'm going to ask you to listen to the questions and answer them specifically and we'll get to other questions later, but the question was: Who are the other parties to the war? And just list them. It has nothing to do with the previous question I asked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The other parties specifically to this war were the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Serbs, and the Serb forces from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And did those parties that you listed also have, to your knowledge, an anti-warfare -- anti-electronic warfare unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I have specific and reliable information that the Bosnian Serbs did indeed have such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the other parties? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you, sir, to briefly explain to us or describe how communicates are made and what you look for in terms of intercepting such communications.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The frequency that we listened to must first be caught or found. In addition to the frequency bearer, you notice the pilot and the characteristic signal which is typical of radio relay equipment. Furthermore, there is the wave bearer, which means that the channels follow a certain order according to their characteristics. What we are talking about is a rather large radio relay equipment with smaller radio relay equipment. You have one channel only and the bearer wave, the so-called bearer wave. What I've been explaining so far really means the following: We adjust our head phones, our headset, and as soon as we notice a signal, we stop right there and we start our recording device, the UHER, the so-called UHER. And that's how you record a conversation or rather tape record a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And just for clarity, a UHER is a type of tape recorder. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's a tape recorder, a UHER.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I'm going to be asking that we go into private session for three more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to show you a map marked P-318 and I'll be asking you a few questions in relation to that map. I thank Madam Usher for assisting us in putting that on the ELMO. Now, I'd like you, sir, to take a look at the map that is on the overhead projector which is right next to you and point to where you and your men were located during this period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And where are you pointing to, sir, can you just indicate what that location is, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: It's elevation 815 station.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that's at Okresanica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, we don't need to look at the map at this time, thanks. Were there other units, sir, besides your own which were engaged in monitoring enemy communications at this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: You said in this location --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, maybe --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Meaning Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask you a more general question first. To your knowledge, do you know whether or not there were other enemy -- sorry, other units besides your own which were involved in monitoring enemy communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, in other locations. We had another unit in Konjuh, the same kind of unit. In Okresanica, we had other units that were involved in the same kind of activity. One of them was a lower-ranking unit attached to a division, to the 21st Division, it was a division unit, and there was a unit of the civilian authorities there, too, the state security.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can you briefly, sir, explain how many people worked on a shift and how many shifts did you work in in your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: A shift can mean two things. You can have the men or the entire team rotating. We would take shifts every ten days. A working shift would usually last between four and eight hours as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to now show you, sir, an exhibit marked P-346 which is under -- which I'll be asking to tender under seal, Your Honour, so I won't be asking that it be placed on the ELMO. If it can simply be shown to the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa, I think that first you showed us a piece of paper with the witness's name on it. What's the number for that? Would you please make a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes. I thank, Your Honour. I may have made a mistake. I apologise, Your Honour. The exhibit that I'm showing to the witness right now is P-346 and the one that has the witness's name on it is Exhibit P-349.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, that exhibit will remain under seal. I understand that at some point you compiled a list in which you identified the names of individuals who served in your group intercepting radio communications. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Are those people listed in that list members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. These are precisely the persons who were members of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't really have any further need for that exhibit. Thank you, Madam Usher. Now, sir, can you tell us how long your platoon had been stationed at Okresanica intercepting communications before July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Our platoon was there from the 10th or 11th of November 1993. I know that we arrived back in 1992, or rather, excuse me, the 10th of October was when we arrived at the feature and then the 11th was the recorded date. That's why I'm saying the 10th or the 11th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And from the position of Okresanica, sir, whose communications were you monitoring? And perhaps if it assists you, we can refer back to the map, but if you don't need it, perhaps you can just answer the question. Which area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: We had so-called zones of responsibility for monitoring for surveillance. Those included the zone of the Drina Corps, the Ozren, the Majevica, and for a while we had -- I'm not sure if it was considered Central Bosnia. It was the area around Tesanj, Maglaj, that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And specifically, sir, who were you monitoring during that period of time, the communications of which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: We were monitoring the communications of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, in the course of intercepting conversations of the enemy, sir, are you familiar with deciphering codes or coded language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: First of all, we would encounter code names of those participating. Some persons could introduce themselves in code and there were whole texts or, rather, bits of communications that were coded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that the witness has to be certified as some kind of expert in decoding before he can go into the testimony of recognising codes. And the question of Ms. Issa was: Are you an expert in decoding and he didn't answer the question first as a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think for the past 45 minutes, Ms. Issa asked the background of this witness, and this witness told us his job, his work, his profession. I think that's sufficient enough for him to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I believe that there's a big difference in radio and communication expertise and encryption and decoding and deciphering codes as an expertise. I would just like to ask Ms. Issa lay the foundation properly if he's going to represent himself as someone who understands how to decode information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, certainly I'm not an expert in this area. But in my view, the foundation is enough. Ms. Issa, are there any more foundations you would like to lay in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, no. Your Honour, I believe the witness has indicated that he is familiar with coded names. I may just ask a few more questions to have him elaborate on his previous answer. In my submission, I believe that the foundation has been properly laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra. We'll listen to whatever the witness is going to tell us, then we'll see whether he's an expert or not. Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to say before I proceed, I'm not putting the witness forward as an expert necessarily. I think Your Honour understands that. I just think that the word expert was used by my friend and I haven't used it. I just want to clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The expert has special meanings and a different person has different interpretations of that word. Let's not debate on the meaning of that word.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you specifically familiar with the coded names of the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And how did you become familiar with these names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Through telephone conversations that they had among themselves. Instead of referring to a specific location, they would provide code names so that we wouldn't know where they were calling from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, I'm going to be asking the usher to place Exhibit P-321 on the overhead projector. And I'll be asking you some questions in relation to this particular map. Now, sir, you've seen this map before in my office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Using your pointer, sir, can you please tell the Judges what this particular exhibit represents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: This map represents the radio relay communications of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask you to point at that at this point, sir, because we weren't able to see it earlier. Where were you pointing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that's the radio relay centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: This is the radio relay centre, yes, of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And it appears to be that it's marked with the word "panorama." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, the word "panorama."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't mean to interrupt the flow of the direct. However, we're going into the details of the map without any foundation as to who marked this map. I think once we get that, then we can go into the specifics so we have a clear record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa. These are the questions also in our mind. You have to lay some foundations first, then you can use this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, do you know how this map was marked or how it came about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I do. The marks were inserted, or rather, we inserted the marks here. We assigned the marks and they were inserted by the organ of the anti-warfare -- electronic anti-warfare unit that I belonged to. It was our own operations centre. We had our own operations centre that was part of the command, but the operations centre not of the corps, the operations centre of my unit, of my company, of the anti-electronic warfare unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Perhaps we can now go through the map. I notice there, sir, where you pointed to the radio relay centre the word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. Also, he just said "we." That is an indefinite term. Can he specify as to whether the commander marked it, whether operators marked it. We still don't know who drew the lines, the vectors, the frequencies. And I think an improper foundation has been laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's a relevant objection. Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned earlier, sir, that "We prepared the map." Who were you referring to when you said "we"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I was referring to the unit that I commanded. Also there were certain elements that would be added or attached from another unit of the same kind that was in a different location.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Did you participate, sir, in getting that information on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I participated directly in obtaining this information, but not in inserting this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you recognise the map as the information that you have obtained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. All these are code names that we encountered in our conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I believe that the witness just referred to another group that really put input into this map. I think he's referring to not only his unit but the map was also marked and created by the MUP or the secret service that was located in his building. I don't believe that this witness, other than understanding the information in the map, had anything to do with the creation, and he has not specified who made the markings on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Or when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the witness answered that question very clearly. I think in your objections you provide additional information which may be a subject in your cross-examination at a later stage. Please let us move on. Yes, Ms. Issa, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, we were dealing with the radio relay centre and you pointed to the term "panorama" as the location of the radio relay centre earlier. Can you tell us, sir, what that term "panorama" refers to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The word "panorama" is a code name for the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And was it close to any particular town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. It was very close to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And can you point to Han Pijesak for us on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And where was the command centre for the Bosnian Serb army located, sir? Can you just say it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: In Han Pijesak, in Han Pijesak, that's where the Main Staff was, but the radio relay centre was at a nearby elevation, which was the usual way to go about it. That's what we all did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can you explain to us, sir, the various features of the map, the links?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The radio relay centre had a number of -- this is a radio relay centre of an entire army, in this case the Army of Republika Srpska. They had radio relay communications with lower-ranking participants, of course the brigades, even lower-ranking units than that. The reason was that they were on the lookout for the best possible conditions to establish links. That's why it comes in this order. We can see other participants, too. The first grade below are the corps and here we see one of the participants, the Drina Corps, for example, the code name is ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And sorry, could you just point that back to that point where you were pointing to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: This place, the code name was "Zlatar" and it was located in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Are there any brigades or any subordinate units that had established links with the command centre? Could you point those out, for us please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Those were the brigades. For example, the Milici Brigade, the code name "Gric Vrelo." There was the Bratunac Brigade, code name "Badem." And several others, too. These were the important ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Do you see the Zvornik Brigade on there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I can't locate it at the moment, but it should be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The angle from which I'm looking at the map at the moment is very inconvenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if it's more convenient for you, sir, if you want you can just take the map off the ELMO and take a look at it. Have you found it now, sir. Just put the map back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just point that out for us, please. And what's the code name for the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade and the code name is "Palma."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I'm finished with that map. Thank you very much. Now, I'm just going to show you, sir, Exhibit P-312 and ask you to identify it. We can actually put that exhibit on the ELMO, please. Now, sir, did you have an opportunity to see this exhibit in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you describe what the exhibit is, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: This is a list of code names identifying the participants.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Does it accurately identify the code name with the corresponding unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. It shows you the code names and their real names, the names of the units using the respective code names.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I think I'm finished with that exhibit, Madam Usher. Can you describe for us, sir, how you -- precisely how you and your unit captured radio communications. If you can describe the process.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: To keep things clear, first there would be an order that was issued to us at the feature. First we would redirect our aerials or antenna in the given direction. We would look for participants. We would use our information to obtain the frequencies that we had had before to see whether those were active at the moment, whether they had any new frequencies, whether there were new participants using the frequencies, and so on and so forth. So first you place the frequencies, and then you go on for a more detailed kind of activity that was usually done at night. There would be a large amount of interference, noise in the communication lines during the day, and the night was much better for that. There were sometimes very small signals that were disguised or masked, and the signals that we monitored were far more powerful than those signals, but sometimes we could even pick up the very small ones and use them to obtain information. Once you've located the participants, the procedure itself was very simple. Sometimes we would pick up certain frequencies that we had given to the command and hen they would send them back to us. So that was the beginning of the whole process. Once that was done, we would start using our earphones and start our shift. We were simply waiting for someone to start talking and then we would tape record those conversations in the way I've described before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And once you tape recorded a conversation, sir, what would you then do with that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Once a conversation was tape recorded, in as for as possible, it needed to be transcribed. What that means is you used a sound recording and you made some sort of transcript out of it. That's what we did. If you want to know more, once we had the information filed, we would send it, send it in the form of a written report to the command on a daily basis. That's within the 24 hours of a single day, but sometimes you would have more reports in a single day, depending on the quantity of information coming in.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just take it step by step and start with the transcription process. Can you describe how you would go about transcribing a conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: It's a very arduous process. We were well trained and we had well-trained ears, our ears were trained to recognise a myriad of different sounds and to distinguish them. Sometimes this would take a whole lot of time, despite all our training. Sometimes there would be a single word we weren't sure about it, so we would just play and replay it 10, 12, 15 times. It was a bit like a deejay's job. The person operating the tape recorder would play it back. We would clean the tape recorder to get the sound as clear as possible. We needed technicians for that position. We would run and rerun the same word, the same sound, in order to be able to identify it with 100 per cent certainty. It sometimes happened that we couldn't get a word-for-word transcript of a certain conversation. So sometimes you had to play the tape back and play several times certain sections of the text itself, of the conversation. Then sometimes the people in the room next door would hear that we were having trouble with one particular portion of the conversation, so then those people would come over to our room and help us try to get this single word right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And why was it so important, sir, to ensure the accuracy of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: It was in the nature of our job that we could not know the meaning of certain words or of a single word being used and we couldn't tell how important a certain word could be, therefore, you had to go into as much detail as possible to submit this information to our command in order to avoid misrepresenting the enemy forces to our command. We were afraid of making any large mistakes. That was the first thing. And secondly, the nature of our activity required us to do our job as thoroughly as possible. Also, there were cases where someone else was monitoring, too. As soon as we had any indication of that, we would sometimes expect this other party to provide more accurate information. So that's how we tried to do our job as thoroughly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say, "Someone else monitoring, too," are you referring to someone else in a different unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: All the units that could be involved in this same kind of activity were in a position to monitor the same frequency that we were. Maybe for a different reason or maybe they were monitoring other channels, but they were obtaining the same text, the same text conversation that we were processing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And just to clarify, sir, did that always happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Well, of course not. But how could we know when it would?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us earlier, sir, that your unit had been at the mountain top at Okresanica listening to the Bosnian Serb military communications for approximately two years. Can you tell us, sir, based on your experience, whether you were able to identify the voices you listened to, specific speakers in the radio communications that you intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The more times we heard a particular participant, the more accurate we could be in terms of determining whether that was the person involved in the conversation. But after several times, it wouldn't be difficult at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us, sir, whether there was any other way for you, besides the ability to recognise the speakers, to identify the men who were communicating or the people who were communicating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Well, of course. There were the names of localities or the code names that they had given, and then they introduced themselves by these names. And in the previous texts, we had their names and these same voices.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And just again, sir, to clarify, you say that there were the names of the localities and the code names. Were there any other names that were given besides the names of the localities and the code names, that you recollect or that you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: We've already discussed this. I said once that the speakers introduced themselves by some code names.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned, sir, that the intercepted communication was transcribed verbatim somewhere. Can you tell us where the intercepted communications were written down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The intercepted communications were transcribed in the unit where we did this. When I say "we," it pertains to the list of these persons that I showed you. So it was not only I, but we all did this. It was a matter of routine procedure. So once this material was transcribed, or rather, once the sound was transmitted into written recordings, then it was entered in a computer. And then in the form of a daily report, it went to the command of our company which was within the corps headquarters. Then the notebooks, the materials that were used up were then put away in my safe -- I'm sorry about the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But before --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I haven't finished yet. Waiting for the shift, these materials went to our headquarters and then when tapes were fully recorded, then we would get new ones and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Just before we stop for the morning recess, sir, I just want to ask you specifically where you wrote down the conversations before we get to sending them on the computer printout to the command. What did you write them in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: We wrote this down in the notebooks that you have. 30-odd notebooks of this type.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be an appropriate time to take the morning recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll break until quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Please accept our apologies for being a few minutes late. We were in the hall and didn't realise the time. No excuse. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Issa, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Before the break, sir, we left off where you were telling us that you and members of your unit transcribed the conversations verbatim into notebooks. Now, after communications were written down in notebooks, can you describe what the next step is in the procedure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The next step in the procedure was that these materials that you've just referred to would be transferred from the notebook into the computer. This was done by the operator at the KZU. These same conversations were then transmitted via computer to the command, to headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And you just mentioned, sir, an operator at the KZU. Can you tell us what the KZU is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: That is the person who encrypted texts in a certain way, sent these texts as protected, encrypted texts to the headquarters of our unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And when the calls were initially transcribed into the notebooks, when they were handwritten down, can you tell us when that took place in relation to when the call was heard or intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: If I understood the question correctly, if we are talking about the time of the conversation, the time of the conversation would be registered and the counter would always placed at 0 before the next conversation would be taped or a few conversations that followed one after the other, then they would be registered as such. So it was the time, the frequency, the channel, if the device has that as well, as also the participants in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, since we're talking about those factors, where would they be registered, the time, the participants, the frequency, and channel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: If there was one conversation and if it could be heard clearly who the participants were, then the time, channel, frequency, and participant would be registered. If that was not clear, then it would be put on a piece of paper. And then when the text would be written down, then the participants would be transmitted into the notebook when the next was copied into the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And if it was clear, initially where would it be registered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: First of all, they would be written down on a piece of paper -- oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I see what you mean. If it was clear, then it would be written down in the notebook first of all. So if it was an easy conversation, so to speak, then it would be written down, the text that is. And then if it could not be fully written down, then the previous part would be checked and then they would be written down later. So there were some conversations that were actually recorded, written down, while they were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And if they were recorded later, when would they be recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: If they were recorded later, then they would be recorded, written down, on a piece of paper. So all conversations, one after the other, would be written down as such in the notebook, in the same order, that is. The first conversation, let me note this in particular, in such a case would be with the counter placed at zero. I mean, it is the counter of the device that I mentioned, that is the UHER, the tape recorder. Its counter would be placed at zero first.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And you're now referring to the time of the conversation when you're talking about the counter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: When talking about the counter, that means the number that a particular conversation took on a particular tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. If I can then just clarify or repeat what I understand you to have said. You told us that the time, the frequency, and the channel, and the participants would sometimes be written on a piece of paper. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But in response to your previous question, you mentioned the time. We had the time directly displayed on the small device that is called the carrier of frequency, the so-called terrace of the radio relay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll -- we will get to that. When you recorded the actual text of the conversations, you told us earlier, sir, that you recorded them in notebooks. Can you tell us when you would write those -- the text of the conversation in the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarity in the record, if we could refer to the actual recording of conversations as recording and the actual writing down of conversations as transcription, otherwise the record is very confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I believe that Ms. Issa is asking a very general question and laying if foundations of the situation. And later on she will lead us to that particular conversation or any particular notes in that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm just talking about general terms, because transcription is the writing down. Recording is the reel-to-reel audio recording of something. She said "You recorded it on pieces of paper." I think just for clarity in the record, we should use "recording" for the audio recording and "transcription" for the written recordings of the conversations. It would make the record clear for everybody, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: To me there is no problem, but if you wish, maybe Ms. Issa, you could try to distinguish the two different ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'll attempt to do that, Your Honour. But at this point we're simply speaking about notebooks, so I do think it's clear. But I'll certainly endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you or members of your unit would hear a call and then subsequently transcribe it in the notebook, can you tell us when you would transcribe it in the notebook in relation to the -- when the conversation was first heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I can. The conversations -- well, it depended on the quantity involved. They could be transmitted in their regular version, as it was called, by the end of the day. So that had to be typed out by 9.00 p.m. or 10.00 p.m. or by 2400 hours. When we had a lot of such material, then we would deviate from this basic version; namely, that we would send this report as we sent regular reports by the end of the day. It could be sent even later, even throughout the night, if necessary. But in principle, if there was a lot of material, then it would be typed out immediately. This went on incessantly. It was typed out as soon as it arrived from the room where we were doing the transcribing of these texts and then it to the computer for encryption and in that case it would go straight away as a report, as a special report to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And why was it necessary, sir, to type out the conversations the same day that they came in and send them to the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: First of all, this pertains to the period during which there were some operations going on, when something was going on. And if necessary, even the command headquarters would require something from us. We would not know why at the time, but we would act accordingly and there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm now, sir, going to show you a particular notebook marked as Exhibit P-322 and ask you if you can identify it for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, I'm going to be showing the witness the original notebook that ultimately we will be tendering copies of the notebooks. And I believe that the notebook -- Your Honours do have copies of the notebooks at this point and I'll be referring to particular pages within the notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are we furnished with the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. It's in the binder that was -- that I believe you were furnished with, the two intercept binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I believe it's in volume 1, but I will check that for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a notebook that was put together by my unit. It bears my signature and there's a certain amount of handwriting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And, sir, when you were in my office you've seen this notebook when we met the other day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, you reviewed several other notebooks in my office that also came from your unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Does this notebook -- you indicated that it contains the conversations that were recorded by members of your staff. Were these conversations -- the written records of the intercepted conversations contained in this notebook, were they made at the time you intercepted the communication? Just generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Well, straight away or at the time, that's a very relative concept. In as far as that was possible. It could have been right then and there and sometimes after the end of the actual conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And were the notebooks that you referred to earlier, the 30-odd notebooks, were they kept by the army as part of their regular business? I'm just asking you a general question. It's not referring to this particular notebook right now, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. It was the army's document. They recorded these in the warehouse of our unit as a document that had also been registered else where. It had a list of contents. It had its own number and the date, the date when the notebook was supposed to be sent to the location. It was specified -- a document was specified to be sent to a location.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And was that the case with the other notebooks as well, sir, that came from your unit in general terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: In general terms, yes. However, there was a possibility, for example, that one of the notebooks didn't have a mark like this, but most of the notebooks needed to have these markings, if not all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to ask you, sir, to turn to a specific page in the notebook that you have in front of you. And perhaps Madam Usher can assist you with that and I'm looking at page 00778904.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, the handwriting on that page, sir, is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. This is certainly my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Is that a conversation that you personally intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, which means that I was the one that transcribed it, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. And did you faithfully transcribe this conversation verbatim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Perhaps at this point, Your Honours, I'm going to read into the regard the conversation. I'll be asking some more questions about it after I do that. And I will simply ask that the English translation, which I believe is at Exhibit 231/E be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey was quite adamant and agitated at me reading documents into the record. We now have his junior colleague coming in here and doing it. I would like to know what is the procedure. The gentleman can read it if he wishes. If we wants to point to a particular area, that's fine. We can all read. I just want some clarification because if I start reading documents and I get a Prosecutor agitated and jumping up and down and screaming at me, I would like to know what the procedure is. That's all

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, did I ever stop you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, you did not. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It depends on the situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to know the rules of the road. If we're going to allow this procedure now, I don't have a problem with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the reading of a document is allowed in the proceedings. This is first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But the parties should try their best to avoid this practice, because that consumes a lot of time. If we could find some other way out, that's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might just indicate that the intercepts are a little different from what I think Mr. Karnavas might be referring to. I think it's a different context and I don't have too much to read into the record. But if I may be just permitted to proceed in this fashion for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It would be of great assistance to the Defence for Mr. Jokic at the moment, because we only have a B/C/S version of it. We would really advocate Ms. Issa reading it so we can have an English translation of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Well, Ms. Issa, you may do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I think, just to assist Ms. Sinatra, it's probably contained in the binder that she has there in front of her and I think she may have found it, the English translation, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It is listed as another P number that was not present at the time. So we do have both documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Anyway, Ms. Issa will read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: For ease of reference, Your Honour, it's in binder number 1, under the July 14th date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We found it. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It starts off with, "7847, channel 5 at 2056 hours. Major General Jovanovic and X." X: Just a moment, to Colonel Vukovic. M: Good evening. X: Evening. M: How is it going? X: We are fine, how about you? M: How can I find out where General Zivanovic is? I've been waiting here for him on his orders since 1700 hours. X: He's here. M: What? X: He's here. M: There. X: Yes. M: Put me through to him. X: I'll try now. Z: Yes? M: Good evening. Z: Good evening, Vuko. M: Things are good here. I did everything in the spirit of what I received last night. And this morning he called me Natasku and I came here this morning at around 10.00 and I -- Z: Major. M: Yes, yes, I understand you. Z: I just came from the checkpoint ... M: Could you repeat that, please. Z: I asked that paper which was sent - there is one - from Blagojevic, about me. M: Okay. Z: Read my conclusions. M: I understand. Z: Because -- (from here on drowned out by previously recorded conversation). M: I understand, completely, and then we'll focus on the one down there. M: I understand. I'm going to my post up there. Z: Listen. Where up there are your boys? M: Well, my boys are now in the western part, working there as of today. Everything's in place, sweet as a nut. Z: Excellent. M: I did that today. Z: (Mumbles something) M: I understand. Z: Take care. M: Take care. Now, sir, did you -- was this document -- was this conversation typed out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, so I don't need to interrupt the proceedings any further. I just still maintain the running objections to the admissibility of any intercepts until this procedure is over with with the witnesses. Although she did read it into record, it has not been determined that it is admissible or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we will deal with the admissibility at a later stage and we well understand your running objections on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, after you transcribed this conversation was it typed out and sent to the command in the manner that you described to us earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: This text was written down immediately and sent to the command immediately. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm going to, sir, refer you now to Prosecution Exhibit 231/E and ask you to identify that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And while Madam Usher is getting the document, Your Honour, I believe the particular conversation I referred to is at P-231 and I misspoke earlier when I referred to as 231/E.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, can you identify, sir -- perhaps we can put that on the ELMO. Can you identify for us, sir, what this document is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: This document is this same text that was typed up. I found one small detail here. It's about the dialect being used, the Ekavica dialect. In the original when the conversation was intercepted, they were speaking in the Ekavica dialect. And the way it was typed up was different. That's the only difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, can you -- looking at the typed-out version that I just handed to you, can you tell us what the date of the conversation was? I'm referring to the document that's on the overhead projector, sir. What is the date that the conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. It's the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned that there was this slight difference in the conversation between the notebook and the computer printout. It's a different spelling, I believe, is that what you were telling us of one word? You have to answer into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the record, sir, what was the word?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you just give me a little bit of time to compare these so then I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Right here in the text, the typed-up version reads the major as saying: "Yes, yes, I understand you."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And what does the handwritten version read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: "Yes, yes, I understand you."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It's just simply a different dialect. That's what you're telling us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, sir, you indicated that you wrote the conversation down in the notebook. Did you also type it up or did somebody else do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I wasn't the one who typed them up. I did transcribe this conversation first. I listened to it and then I transcribed it. The conversation was typed up by the encryption operator. In the unit itself at the location itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the date of 14 July that is on that computer printout, 1995, can you explain how that date is generated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: This date was automatically inserted by the computer. It was always computerised for daily reports and for reports like this one. For all reports, the date was inserted by the computer. And that was why we didn't leave the date in our notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Turning then to the next conversation in a notebook marked as Exhibit 323.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I believe, Your Honours, this is also in the same location in the intercept binders that you were provided with earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And what's the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: The date is 14 July, 1995, Your Honour, and the particular conversation I will be referring to momentarily is at P-232.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you recognise that notebook. It's also a notebook that you've seen earlier in my office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. This is a notebook that was drafted in my unit in the very period of time that it refers to. The handwriting on the cover is my own handwriting. The handwriting on page 1 is my own handwriting. There is a file number given by my unit and my signature, my signature testifying to the fact that the notebook was sent on and that it contains a list.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And that's found at the very back of the notebook. Is that correct, your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like you, sir, to turn to page 00779705 of the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I'm referring again, Your Honours, to P-232 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It should be slash B.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Perhaps it is, Your Honour. I appreciate the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And again, I would ask that the -- a copy of the English translation, which is at 232/A be placed on the ELMO. Now, sir, turning to that page, is that -- you indicated that's your handwriting on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Is that a conversation that you personally intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. I personally recorded and transcribed this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And did you faithfully record the conversation verbatim into the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. Word for word. In as for as I could hear and actually understand what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, I can now read out what is on the ELMO, the English translation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object because it is time consuming, we can all read. If they want -- if she wishes to direct the gentleman to a particular portion of the intercept, I certainly have no objections. It is going to be introduced, I assume, or tendered, so -- but I don't see why Ms. Issa is going to be reading an entire document on direct unless she can establish the basis for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think everybody has got that document at our hands. If you have some particular paragraph you want to mention, you could read that particular paragraph, but there's no need to read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I won't do that, but I indicated earlier it was only two documents or two conversations I was going through. But if Your Honour doesn't wish me to do that, then I will ask for specific questions in relation to the conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please ask some specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've read this conversation to refresh your memory when you were in my office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And perhaps if I can just refer you to the time the conversation took place, sir, what time was that? If you can just refer either to the notebook or to the ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The conversation I'm looking at took place at 2102.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And there's a notation here, sir, that says: "Palma duty officer." If we can then deal with that term. Can you tell us what Palma is associated with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Palma is one of the codes from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: It's -- it refers to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And what about Badem. Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Badem, I'm not sure if it's Bratunac or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just in looking at the conversation, sir, I note here that there are some dots after particular -- or before a particular statement made by one of the parties. Can you tell us what the dots represent in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: These dots are parts of the conversation that we couldn't make out. Meanwhile, there was a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Is there anything particular about this conversation that you recollect that was perhaps slightly unusual?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, I don't mean to object, but there's a foundational question, does he recollect this conversation, first of all. Then if he does recollect the conversation, then he can continue. The other thing is, I would like to know is this based on his independent memory or is it based on his memory being refreshed from this document? If he doesn't recollect it, then I guess there's no sense in going on to the next step and that is for him to describe what indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we have been on this document for quite some minutes already. I think there is no problem that the witness recollects that was the note he took. And as for the second objection -- well, Ms. Issa, you may ask some questions in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just to make things clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I will do that, Your Honour. Perhaps if I can keep going in this line of questioning and I'll get to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, is there anything unusual about the conversation that you recollect, this particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, he hasn't established that he recollects having this conversation. I'm not suggesting that he didn't write it down. This is his handwriting and he stated that it was his handwriting, but he hasn't indicating recollecting this particular conversation. You know, we're talking years later, many different conversations. Now, if he can point to something having read it that he recollects something in particular, I have no objection. But here she's assuming a fact that's not in evidence as if he recollects something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is that an important issue? I don't see where you're going, Mr. Karnavas. So long as we have the notebook here and the witness recognises it's his handwriting, I don't think there's any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think there is a problem if there's a suggestion that he recollects this particular conversation. Obviously he's recorded it. It may be the case that he recognises his handwriting but he doesn't recollect that particular conversation because it never registered in his mind. There was nothing significant about it. This particular conversation may have some significance to him. And if that's the case, I would like to know how it is that he would recognise this particular conversation. So it's a foundational question. I believe the question is being asked and the way it's framed, it suggests that he does indeed recollect something. He hasn't said that he recollects the conversation or anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As I said, we have been working on this document for quite a few minutes already. So I don't think your objections here are relevant because the witness has already been reminded at least of this conversation by the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Very well. I accept the Court's ruling. I'll go that far. I accept the Court's ruling and I will abide by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry, but we do support Mr. Karnavas's objection. The record only reflects that he has refreshed his memory in the Prosecutor's office before testifying. It doesn't reflect that he recalls or remembers from personal knowledge this conversation. I think there is a big distinction there. The question needs to be: Does he recollect this? Why? What makes it stand out? Not that he refreshed his memory empty Prosecutor's office before testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa has already promised us she will ask some questions in this aspect at a later stage. I hope you also support Mr. Karnavas's attitude that accept the rulings of this Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. You may proceed, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, sir? Do you remember what I just asked you? Do you want me to re-ask the question perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: It's not necessary. In spite of all these objections, I remember the question and I remember what was in my own memory. This was so characteristic, this remark that was made, and this remained in my memory, that there was such a text. And this made it possible for us because the telephone operator left the line open, so we heard the conversation in the room itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And when you are referring to the telephone operator, which telephone operator are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: It refers to the telephone operator, the person from the telephone exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And if you can just clarify what was -- you indicated that the telephone operator left the line open and allowed you to hear the conversation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He left the line open so we could hear the X, Y participants. We did not know anything else except for the part of the conversation that is here, you see. And that is how it reached our device.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know, sir, the location of the telephone operator who left the line open?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The operator from Badem.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to direct your attention, sir, to a particular portion of the conversation and to clarify matters, I'm just going to read out this particular portion, Your Honour, with Your Honour's permission. And I also just note that the translation is on the monitor, on the overhead projector. Starting with the top it says: : Hello, Badem. Let me talk to Beara. B: Who wants to talk to him? : The Palma duty officer wants to talk to him. Beara is needed urgently, somebody needs him. The superior command urgently needs him but he has to call me. It's literally translated as the "higher house," I believe in this conversation. B: Okay. P: Okay. What? Give me Beara, don't hang up. J: Hello, who is it, Major, I'm the duty officer at Palma, I need Beara urgently. This is Major Jokic, who is that? Why, expletive, are you not answering? Is Ostoja there? Is Brko there? Don't, another expletive, around, the line has to be free and you must pick it up right away. Who is Ostoja? Is Ostoja there? Have him call me urgently. I will, I will. Hello. Hello. Now, directing your attention to this particular portion of the conversation, sir, was there anything at the time when you were listening to this conversation that you were uncertain about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Specifically, because I see that the conversation was taken down straight away, I can see that I put it down immediately. As we listened to it, there was the problem of how logical it was for the same participant to be saying all of this and when listening to it again, we realised that that's the way it was. It was a single speaker saying all of this. And he did not leave very long breaks. So that is why we did not put in dots. So it was all with very short breaks, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, directing you specifically to the last portion of the conversation, "I will, I will. Hello, hello." Is that the portion of the conversation that you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. When you read this conversation, you have the impression that there are other participants in this conversation. However, it is one single participant giving an answer to someone who we cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And is it only that portion, the "I will, I will, hello hello," of this statement that you are referring to or is there any other part of the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It's a leading. It's a leading fashion question. She can ask him to identify it exactly. The gentleman seems to understand what he's reading. She can point him and ask him how, what, why, when, these sorts of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
