utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, you are right. It is leading. You may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I was simply trying to speed things along, Your Honour. I didn't think it was in dispute, but I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would kindly ask counsel, once a ruling is made, to please accept it and just move on rather than to editorialise because it causes me to then have to respond. This is direct examination. She is a Prosecutor. She should know how to do direct. That's all I'm asking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think Ms. Issa is editorialising anything. But anyway, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, which portion of the conversation you were referring to specifically. Perhaps you can just read it out. Just that portion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Well, there are swear words there too. How can I read that now?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to read out the swear words. I'm just talking about that particular statement that you told us about earlier that you said initially you thought may have been from another speaker. You don't have to read out the whole thing, just the one sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The entire part before, "Have him call me urgently." And then it says, "I will, I will, hello. Hello." That is what it refers to. All the rest is all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But just to clarify, sir, the question that was raised in your mind at the time, what specifically did that relate to? Which words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The following words: "I will, I will. Hello. Hello."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Was there any similar question with respect to any other part of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And how many times did you listen to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but several times at any rate, meaning more than once.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, turning then to Prosecution Exhibit 232/E, I'm going to ask you if you recognise that. Perhaps we can put it on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, it will be folded over to conceal the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, if you can look at the overhead projector that's next to you, the machine that is right next to you or on the screen. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. That's the document that is in the notebook in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And is that the typed version of the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, when this typed version was typed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: This was typed on the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And when did you intercept the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Was this computer printout also sent to your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that had priority, and that's how it was sent to the command. So the time had to be the briefest possible, the time that we had it in our hands while it was taking down, typed out and put on the computer, and forwarded to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I just have a few more questions, sir, that don't relate to the document, so I'm going to ask Madam Usher to take the notebooks away for now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And perhaps, Your Honour, while I'm asking these clean-up questions, I would offer the notebooks to Your Honours, the original versions, if Your Honours would like to take a look at them and also if the Defence wants to take a look at them they're certainly welcome to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would like to have at the next break the opportunity to inspect the original notebook, but we will use the time at the break if the Court will allow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. After the break, I think you could show that notebook to the Defence team as well as to the legal assistants of the Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, but I don't know if Your Honour wishes to see it now. If you don't, I will certainly wait until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe after would be better so that we could save some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were intercepting conversations, did you share your information with anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Intercepted conversations, if a unit or if the civilian authority from the state security, if they asked to look at it on a computer, we would give it to them on a diskette so they would see if there was anything there for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And have you seen copy -- would they prepare a report containing the information you shared with them, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. What did you do with the notebook, sir, once each notebook was filled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I would put them in the safe in my room and when the first shift would take place, that is to say, when people would leave the actual location, then the commander of my company would come, this was one of his duties. And if he was absent, then this could be done by the other officers or the head of the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And they would take the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: Yes. They would take the notebooks and they would give us empty ones so that we could go on working, although this is not directly related. It's not that we didn't have any, but they had on each report what our needs were and that is how they knew that we did not have very many left. And then when necessary, they would bring us new ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just one last question to clarify something, sir. You mentioned earlier that at times another unit, such as the unit at Konjuh, would intercept the same conversation that your unit intercepted. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: I recall that. At one meeting, we discussed a document that was brought from two localities. One of these documents was either incomplete or was not a faithful copy of that conversation, so this was discussed and a request was made for better work to be performed. So that's how this happened. It seemed that there were others who were following this, too, but then from then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And to your knowledge, sir, are conversations that are heard -- if the same conversation is heard by your unit and heard by another unit at Konjuh, is it necessarily heard with the same clarity by your unit or the unit at Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Lack of foundation. It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so. We mentioned other facilities in other places already. Why not ask some questions to this witness to compare the qualities of the recordings?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the witness knows. I don't see how -- a foundation hasn't been laid. I mean, was he working over there? Did he make a comparison so he could answer that particular question. That's all I'm asking, Your Honour. I'm not saying that he's not qualified to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I prefaced my question, Your Honour, with "To your knowledge," so he can tell us if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117
utterances.text: The only thing I don't know is whether the electronic surveillance documents were provided. And what is stated there quite clearly is how strong the signal was at various localities. And this clearly indicates whether there were differences in strength in terms of the signals received at different localities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Issa. Well, Witness, I'm sorry to say that we have to keep you in The Hague for the weekend because we are not sitting tomorrow for the maintenance of this courtroom. And during your stay in The Hague, please do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I think we will resume at Monday afternoon. Yes, the hearing an adjourned.
